title: AI's Capability in Assisting Scientific Research in Physics, Astrophysics, and Cosmology I: Literature Review
tldr: Chatbots find useful papers experts miss, but mid-2025 models get most references' details wrong.
newcomer: This paper is a study of AI tools rather than of physics. To follow it you need a rough idea of how chatbots work and why they invent things, how physicists search the literature, and how a search is scored. The physics of the eight test projects is optional.

sections.name: Language models
sections.summary: What chatbots are, how they are prompted, why they make things up, and how search tools change that.
sections.role: The models under test, and the reasons the authors give for why newer ones are more accurate.

sections.name: Literature search
sections.summary: How physicists find papers, and the identifiers and records that say whether a reference is right.
sections.role: The task itself, the four kinds of reference, and the DOI/Crossref check behind the hallucination results.

sections.name: Judging the results
sections.summary: How to score a search against a reference list, and why relevance judgements are subjective.
sections.role: Explains the overlap and relevance numbers in Table II and the study's caveats.

sections.name: AI in science
sections.summary: From machine learning for simulations to LLMs that review, plan and do research.
sections.role: Places this study in a series testing AI at each step of research.

sections.name: The eight test projects
sections.summary: The physics behind the projects used as test cases, from galaxies to gravitational waves and inflation.
sections.role: Not needed for the results, but helps read the project descriptions and judge the SU(2) comparison.

concepts.name: Large language models
concepts.plain: Neural networks trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word; chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini are built on them.
concepts.why_here: The things being tested: ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini and ChatGPT Pro 5.5.

concepts.name: Prompting
concepts.plain: Telling a model what to do in plain text, with any context it needs; the same prompt can give different answers on different runs or models.
concepts.why_here: Every model got the same standard prompt, filled in with each project's background and goal (Appendix B).

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.plain: When a model states something fluent but false, such as a citation to a paper that doesn't exist.
concepts.why_here: The paper's second question: it splits hallucinated references into fabrications and metadata mismatches.

concepts.name: Retrieval and web search
concepts.plain: Letting a model look things up (a search engine or database) and base its answer on what it finds, rather than on memory alone.
concepts.why_here: All three mid-2025 models had online search; the authors think better search explains why Deep Research made fewer errors.

concepts.name: Tool-using research agents
concepts.plain: Models that plan, search, read and check over many steps before answering, like ChatGPT's Deep Research mode.
concepts.why_here: Deep Research and Pro 5.5 were by far the most reliable; the paper reads this as a property of the model plus its tools.

concepts.name: Test-time compute
concepts.plain: Letting a model spend more computation (longer reasoning, more searches) on each question instead of making the model bigger.
concepts.why_here: One of the authors' explanations for Pro 5.5's perfect references.

concepts.name: Literature reviews
concepts.plain: Finding and reading what has already been done on a topic, to place new work and check that it is original.
concepts.why_here: The research task being tested: the first of four steps in a physics project.

concepts.name: The growth of the literature
concepts.plain: The number of papers published each year keeps rising fast, so no one can read everything in their field.
concepts.why_here: The paper's motivation: the volume of new papers makes it easy to miss important work.

concepts.name: ADS, INSPIRE and arXiv
concepts.plain: The databases physicists use to find papers: NASA ADS for astronomy, INSPIRE for high-energy physics and the arXiv preprint server.
concepts.why_here: The prompt asked models to give ADS, INSPIRE or arXiv links where possible.

concepts.name: DOIs and Crossref metadata
concepts.plain: A DOI is a permanent ID for a paper; Crossref keeps the official record of its title, authors, year and journal.
concepts.why_here: Each AI reference was checked by looking up its DOI in Crossref and comparing the fields.

concepts.name: Kinds of reference
concepts.plain: Reviews give an overview, highly cited papers mark the key results, recent papers the current state, and collaboration papers (Planck, DES, HSC…) the data everyone uses.
concepts.why_here: Both humans and AI sorted their references into these four categories, and matches had to agree on the category.

concepts.name: Fabrications vs metadata mismatches
concepts.plain: A fabricated reference points to a paper that doesn't exist; a mismatched one points to a real paper but gets some details wrong.
concepts.why_here: The paper's two kinds of hallucination: 3% fabrications, 64% mismatches in mid-2025.

concepts.name: Overlap, precision and recall
concepts.plain: Ways to score a search: recall is the share of the right papers you found, precision the share of what you found that is right.
concepts.why_here: 'Found by both', 'human not AI' and 'AI irrelevant' in Table II are versions of these.

concepts.name: Relevance judgements
concepts.plain: Deciding whether a document is useful for a need; different people often disagree, so studies measure how well judges agree.
concepts.why_here: Each expert alone judged whether the AI's papers were relevant; the authors note this is subjective.

concepts.name: Controlled comparisons
concepts.plain: Testing two methods on the same tasks under the same conditions, so differences come from the methods and not the tasks.
concepts.why_here: The study's design: the same eight projects searched in parallel by experts and by LLMs with the same prompt.

concepts.name: Benchmarks for AI in physics
concepts.plain: Standard sets of tasks used to score AI models and track progress over time.
concepts.why_here: The authors say their one-project Pro 5.5 result needs a systematic benchmark to confirm.

concepts.name: Machine learning in physics
concepts.plain: Neural networks used to speed up simulations, find patterns in data and infer physical parameters.
concepts.why_here: The paper's starting point: AI in physics began with numerical work before LLMs arrived.

concepts.name: LLMs as research assistants
concepts.plain: Using chatbots to review papers, plan projects or carry out parts of research.
concepts.why_here: The wider question the paper series asks: can LLMs help at each step of a physics project?

concepts.name: Autonomous AI scientists
concepts.plain: Systems that try to run a whole research project, from idea to paper, with little human help.
concepts.why_here: The authors plan to test project execution and paper writing next.

concepts.name: Cosmology and large-scale structure
concepts.plain: How the universe expands and how matter clumps into a web of galaxies and dark matter halos.
concepts.why_here: Most of the eight test projects (LBG, IA, RG, GW) are about large-scale structure.

concepts.name: Galaxy bias and the halo connection
concepts.plain: Galaxies sit in dark matter halos, so they trace the matter distribution with a 'bias'; the halo occupation distribution says how many galaxies each halo holds.
concepts.why_here: The LBG project; the GW project also estimates a bias for black-hole mergers.

concepts.name: Weak lensing and intrinsic alignments
concepts.plain: Matter bends light and slightly stretches background galaxies; galaxies' own aligned shapes (intrinsic alignments) can mimic that signal.
concepts.why_here: The IA project, and the weak-lensing maps used in the GW project.

concepts.name: Active galactic nuclei
concepts.plain: Galaxies whose central black hole is swallowing gas and shining brightly; they can switch on and off over thousands of years.
concepts.why_here: The AGN duty-cycle project, and the radio galaxies that contaminate CMB maps.

concepts.name: Gravitational waves and pulsar timing
concepts.plain: Ripples in spacetime, seen by LIGO from merging black holes and, at much lower frequencies, by timing many pulsars.
concepts.why_here: The GW and PTA projects; the Hellings–Downs curve is the GR prediction the PTA project tests.

concepts.name: Inflation from vector fields
concepts.plain: A burst of accelerated expansion in the early universe, usually driven by a scalar field; some models use gauge fields instead.
concepts.why_here: The SU(2) project, also used for the Pro 5.5 test: can a massive Yang–Mills or Proca field drive inflation?

concepts.name: Laser ablation and Gaussian processes
concepts.plain: Short laser pulses remove material to carve tiny structures; Gaussian-process regression predicts results between measured settings.
concepts.why_here: The AR project: predicting when debris forms on laser-machined anti-reflection surfaces.

concepts.name: CMB foregrounds and simulations
concepts.plain: Sources between us and the cosmic microwave background, such as radio galaxies, add signal that must be modelled and removed; N-body simulations help.
concepts.why_here: The RG project, built on the HalfDome simulations.
